title: "Co-Movement & Co-Crashes"
subtitle: "Sectors, the correlation block, and the headline statistic"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, BAND, despine
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import einx                      # linear algebra with the axes spelled out
from jaxtyping import Float      # shape annotations: Float[Array, "n_days"]

Array = np.ndarray
R = datasets.load_returns()
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta().set_index("ticker")
BANKS = ["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"]
```

A portfolio's real danger is not that one name falls — it's that **many fall
together**.  This page shows that co-movement directly: which names share a fate,
how the banks form a block, and what the course's headline *co-crash* number
actually counts.

---

## 1 · The Correlation Block

Order the basket by sector and the correlation matrix lights up in blocks.  The
five banks form a bright square (they move almost as one, ~0.77); utilities and
staples sit in a dimmer corner, much less tied to the banks (~0.29) — though, as
the next sections show, a systemic crisis lifts even those cross-sector links.

```{python}
#| label: fig-corr-block
#| fig-cap: "Return correlation matrix, ordered by sector. The bank block (top-left) is uniformly bright — average within-bank correlation ~0.77 — while bank-vs-utility correlation averages ~0.29: far lower, but no longer negligible (the 2008 and 2020 crises couple everything to a degree). Sector membership still predicts co-movement."
order = meta.sort_values("sector").index.tolist()
C = R[order].corr()                              # 14×14 Pearson matrix for the display
C_mat: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = C.values
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 6.2))
im = ax.imshow(C_mat, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_xticklabels(order, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_yticklabels(order, fontsize=8)
# sector dividers
secs = meta.loc[order, "sector"].values
bounds = [i for i in range(1, len(order)) if secs[i] != secs[i - 1]]
for b in bounds:
    ax.axhline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0); ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=INK, lw=1.0)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="correlation")
ax.set_title("Correlation lives in sector blocks", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

That ordering isn't magic — it's just the `sector` column of the basket
metadata. Before the matrix can light up in blocks, the tickers have to be
*grouped* by sector. Here is that grouping made explicit: load the metadata and
collapse it into a plain `sector → tickers` dictionary. Every block in this
chapter (and every block the labs reload) is one entry of this mapping.

```{python}
#| label: sector-grouping
# meta is already loaded in the setup cell, indexed by ticker.
# Re-read it un-indexed so we can group the `ticker` column by `sector`.
meta_flat = datasets.load_basket_meta()
sector_to_tickers = {
    sec: grp["ticker"].tolist()
    for sec, grp in meta_flat.groupby("sector", sort=False)
}
for sec, tickers in sector_to_tickers.items():
    print(f"{sec:10s} → {tickers}")
```

The matrix above is just this dictionary laid end to end: banks, then tech, then
energy, utilities, and staples. The bright squares are the *within*-sector
entries of the mapping; the dimmer off-diagonal rectangles are the *between*-sector
ones. We will lean on exactly this distinction below.

## Blocks: From a Panel to Multidimensional Variables

So far every quantity — a correlation, a co-crash fraction — has been built from
*two scalar columns*. But the correlation matrix already hinted at something
larger: a whole **sector** behaves like one object. Slice those columns out
together and you get a **block** — a multidimensional variable
$X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, where $n$ is the number of trading days and $d$
is the number of names in the sector. A block is not a column; it is a *bundle*
of columns you treat as a single variable.

```{python}
#| label: sector-blocks
# A sector is a block: select all of its columns at once.
X_banks:  Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"]  = R[sector_to_tickers["Banks"]]    # (n_days, 5)
X_tech:   Float[Array, "n_days d_tech"]   = R[sector_to_tickers["Tech"]]     # (n_days, 3)
X_energy: Float[Array, "n_days d_energy"] = R[sector_to_tickers["Energy"]]   # (n_days, 2)

for name, blk in [("X_banks", X_banks), ("X_tech", X_tech), ("X_energy", X_energy)]:
    print(f"{name:9s} shape = {blk.shape}   columns = {list(blk.columns)}")
```

Read the shapes carefully: `X_banks` is `(n_days, 5)` — five real numbers per
day, a point in $\mathbb{R}^5$, not a scalar. That single change of viewpoint
splits every dependence question cleanly in two:

- **Within a block** — *how redundant are the banks?* JPM, BAC, C, WFC and GS
  carry overlapping information; a within-block measure (later: **total
  correlation** $T(X_\text{banks})$) quantifies that shared core.
- **Between blocks** — *how much do banks and energy move together?* That is a
  between-block measure (later: **mutual information** $I(X_\text{banks};
  X_\text{energy})$) — one number summarising a $5 \times 2$ slab of the
  correlation matrix, not a single cell.

Correlation can only ever fill one cell at a time. The information-theoretic
measures in the dependence and gaussianization chapters take a *whole block* as
their argument — which is exactly why those labs need blocks handed to them, not
columns.

### The Real-Toy Block: Two Banks vs Two Energy Majors

The full bank block lives in $\mathbb{R}^5$ — too wide to follow by hand. So we
keep a deliberately small **real-toy block**: two banks against two energy
majors, a real `[x1, x2, y1, y2]` panel you can read row by row. It is real
market data, but small enough to reason about like a toy.

```{python}
#| label: real-toy-block
x: Float[Array, "n_days d_x"] = R[["JPM", "BAC"]]   # block x: two banks      → (n_days, 2)
y: Float[Array, "n_days d_y"] = R[["XOM", "CVX"]]   # block y: two energy majors → (n_days, 2)
toy: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = pd.concat([x, y], axis=1)   # the [JPM, BAC, XOM, CVX] panel
print("x shape =", x.shape, " y shape =", y.shape, " toy shape =", toy.shape)
toy.head().round(4)
```

Now the 4×4 correlation of that little panel. This is the structure the
information labs will later re-derive — and the *ordering* is the whole point:

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-corr-block
#| fig-cap: "The 4×4 correlation block of the real-toy panel [JPM, BAC, XOM, CVX]. Two bright 2×2 squares on the diagonal — within-banks (JPM·BAC ≈ 0.83) and within-energy (XOM·CVX ≈ 0.78) — and a dimmer off-diagonal 2×2 slab coupling banks to energy (≈ 0.35). Read as information: redundancy *within* a sector outweighs the shared signal *between* sectors — the ordering the labs quantify as T(x) within banks > I(x;y) banks↔energy."
# Corr(X) = (1/n)·ZᵀZ   with Z = (X − μ)/σ   (standardize columns, then gram)
M: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = toy.to_numpy()
n_days = M.shape[0]
μ = M.mean(axis=0)                               # per-column mean μⱼ
σ = M.std(axis=0)                                # per-column std σⱼ  (population, ddof=0)
Z: Float[Array, "n_days 4"] = (M - μ) / σ        # standardized columns, ⟨zⱼ⟩=0, Var(zⱼ)=1
Ctoy: Float[Array, "4 4"] = einx.dot("n i, n j -> i j", Z, Z) / n_days   # ρᵢⱼ = (1/n)·zᵢ·zⱼ
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.6))
im = ax.imshow(Ctoy, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(4)); ax.set_xticklabels(toy.columns, fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticks(range(4)); ax.set_yticklabels(toy.columns, fontsize=10)
ax.axhline(1.5, color=INK, lw=1.2); ax.axvline(1.5, color=INK, lw=1.2)  # x | y divider
for i in range(4):
    for j in range(4):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{Ctoy[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center",
                color=INK if abs(Ctoy[i, j]) < 0.6 else "white", fontsize=9)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, label="correlation")
ax.set_title("within-bank & within-energy high,\nbank↔energy lower", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Block vs Column, in One Sentence
A **column** is a scalar variable (one name's return). A **block** is a
multidimensional variable (a sector, or a hand-picked bundle). Pearson
correlation compares columns; the information measures ahead compare *blocks* —
so this chapter's job is to build and hand off the blocks.
:::

## 2 · Co-Movement Up Close: Two Scatters

Correlation is an average over all days.  Zoom into two pairs and the *shape* of
the dependence appears.  Two banks fall on a tight diagonal — and crucially their
points pile into the **lower-left quadrant** (both down hard on the same day).  A
bank and a utility make a diffuse cloud whose danger corner is far sparser —
though, in this crisis-spanning sample, not empty.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatters
#| fig-cap: "Daily returns, JPM vs BAC (two banks) and JPM vs DUK (bank vs utility). The shaded lower-left box is the joint-crash quadrant (both below their 10% tail). It is crowded for the banks (~70% co-crash) and far sparser — but not empty — for the bank-utility pair (~30%). Tail dependence you can see."
def lower_tail_box(ax, x: Float[Array, "n_days"], y: Float[Array, "n_days"], q=0.10):
    tx, ty = np.quantile(x, q), np.quantile(y, q)   # the q-quantile crash lines (qˣ, qʸ)
    ax.axvspan(x.min(), tx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08)
    ax.axhspan(y.min(), ty, color=CRASH, alpha=0.08)
    ax.axvline(tx, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.axhline(ty, color=CRASH, lw=0.8, ls="--")

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))
for ax, b, name in [(axL, "BAC", "two banks"), (axR, "DUK", "bank vs utility")]:
    x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
    y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[b].to_numpy()
    lower_tail_box(ax, x, y)
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none")
    cc = cocrash_fraction(x, y)
    ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel(f"{b} return")
    ax.set_title(f"JPM vs {b} ({name})\nco-crash = {cc:.0%}", fontsize=11)
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 3 · The Co-Crash Number

The statistic the course quotes again and again is the **co-crash fraction**:

> Of the days when one name is in its worst 10%, on what fraction is the *other*
> name also in its worst 10%?

That is `cocrash_fraction(x, y)` — a conditional probability,
$P(Y \text{ crashes} \mid X \text{ crashes})$.  An **independent** pair scores ~10%
(the threshold itself); a co-crashing pair scores far higher.

Before tallying every name, watch the number built on a single pair. Take JPM and
BAC, and shade the **10% of days JPM falls hardest** — that band *is* the
condition. The co-crash fraction is then just a count inside the band: of those
worst-JPM days, how many sit below BAC's crash line too (red), versus how many
BAC shrugged off (blue)?

```{python}
#| label: fig-cocrash-anatomy
#| fig-cap: "Anatomy of one co-crash number (JPM·BAC). The shaded band is the *condition* — the 10% of days JPM falls hardest. Among those days, red points fall below BAC's crash line too (a co-crash) and blue ones do not; their ratio is the co-crash fraction, here ~70%. The bar chart below runs this same tally for every name."
x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["BAC"].to_numpy()
qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(x, 0.10), np.quantile(y, 0.10)   # the 10% crash lines
band: Float[Array, "n_days"] = x <= qˣ                 # condition: JPM in its worst 10%
co:   Float[Array, "n_days"] = band & (y <= qʸ)        # …and BAC craters too → a co-crash
hold: Float[Array, "n_days"] = band & (y > qʸ)         # …but BAC held up
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.0))
ax.axvspan(x.min(), qˣ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
ax.axhline(qʸ, color=INK, lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.scatter(x[~band], y[~band], s=7, c="0.78", alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none")
ax.scatter(x[hold], y[hold], s=26, c=COOL, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"JPM crashes, BAC holds  ({int(hold.sum())})")
ax.scatter(x[co], y[co], s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none",
           label=f"both crash — a co-crash  ({int(co.sum())})")
ax.text(qˣ, ax.get_ylim()[1], "  condition: JPM in its worst 10%",
        color=CRASH, fontsize=9, va="top", ha="left")
ax.text(ax.get_xlim()[1], qʸ, "BAC's crash line  ", color=INK, fontsize=8.5,
        va="bottom", ha="right")
ax.set_xlabel("JPM return"); ax.set_ylabel("BAC return")
ax.set_title(f"Of JPM's {int(band.sum())} worst days, BAC also craters on "
             f"{int(co.sum())}  →  co-crash {int(co.sum()) / int(band.sum()):.0%}",
             fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Run that same tally for **every** name against JPM and the contagion structure
appears:

```{python}
#| label: fig-cocrash-bars
#| fig-cap: "Co-crash fraction of every name with JPM. The other banks land near 65–70% (when JPM has a worst-10% day, so do they). Even defensive utilities sit at ~30% — three times the 10% independence baseline (dashed) — because systemic crises drag everyone down. But the banks still tower over the rest."
cc = (pd.Series({t: cocrash_fraction(R["JPM"].to_numpy(), R[t].to_numpy())
                 for t in R.columns if t != "JPM"})
      .sort_values())
colors = [CRASH if meta.loc[t, "sector"] == "Banks"
          else plotting.PALETTE["green"]
          if meta.loc[t, "sector"] in ("Utilities", "Staples")
          else COOL for t in cc.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ax.barh(cc.index, cc.values * 100, color=colors)
ax.axvline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)")
ax.set_xlabel("co-crash with JPM (%)")
ax.set_title("Banks crash hardest with JPM; defensives aren't immune", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 4 · More Than Correlation Predicts

The 10% line is the wrong yardstick once names are correlated at all — a
correlated pair *should* co-crash more than 10%. The sharper question: more than
a **Gaussian** with that *exact* correlation would? Fit a bivariate normal to
each pair's correlation and ask it the same co-crash question. Every pair beats
it — even the diversified bank-utility pair crashes together more often than its
correlation can account for. That surplus is genuine **tail dependence**: the
part a covariance matrix, and the Gaussian risk model built on it, structurally
misses.

See it on one pair before totalling. Standardise JPM and BAC, then draw a
bivariate Gaussian with their *exact* correlation beside the real cloud:

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-vs-gaussian
#| fig-cap: "Same correlation, two worlds (JPM·BAC). Left: real standardized returns. Right: a bivariate Gaussian fit to that exact correlation, r ≈ 0.83. Same tilt, same ellipse — but the Gaussian barely passes ±4σ, while real crashes sprawl past −10σ and pack the lower-left corner, so the real co-crash (~70%) outruns the Gaussian's (~60%). Axes clipped at ±5σ; the gap is tail dependence."
x: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
y: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["BAC"].to_numpy()
xz: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()   # standardized JPM, z = (x−μ)/σ
yz: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (y - y.mean()) / y.std()   # standardized BAC
ρ = np.corrcoef(xz, yz)[0, 1]                            # the pair's exact correlation
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
g: Float[Array, "n_days 2"] = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, ρ], [ρ, 1]], size=len(xz))
LIM = 5

def _corner(ax, u: Float[Array, "n_days"], v: Float[Array, "n_days"], title):
    qᵘ, qᵛ = np.quantile(u, 0.10), np.quantile(v, 0.10)   # the 10% crash lines
    box: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (u <= qᵘ) & (v <= qᵛ)   # joint lower-tail quadrant
    ax.axvspan(-LIM, qᵘ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)
    ax.axhspan(-LIM, qᵛ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)
    ax.scatter(u[~box], v[~box], s=6, c="0.78", alpha=0.22, edgecolors="none")
    ax.scatter(u[box], v[box], s=13, c=CRASH, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nco-crash = {cocrash_fraction(u, v):.0%}", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlim(-LIM, LIM); ax.set_ylim(-LIM, LIM)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 5.0))
_corner(axL, xz, yz, "Real returns (JPM·BAC, standardized)")
_corner(axR, g[:, 0], g[:, 1], f"A Gaussian, same r = {ρ:.2f}")
fig.suptitle("Same correlation, same tilt — but real losses sprawl into the corner",
             fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The Gaussian is the right shape and the right tilt — it just can't reach the
joint extremes the real corner is full of. Across pairs, that surplus is
everywhere:

```{python}
#| label: fig-excess-tail
#| fig-cap: "Co-crash for three pairs: what a Gaussian fit to the pair's own correlation predicts (blue) versus what actually happens (red), against the 10% independence baseline (dashed). Every real pair lands above its Gaussian — by 6–11 points — so the joint crashing is not just 'they're correlated'. The gap is tail dependence the correlation never sees, and it survives even for the loosely-tied bank-utility pair."
from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal, norm

def gaussian_cocrash(ρ, q=0.10):
    """Co-crash a bivariate normal with this correlation would produce."""
    z = norm.ppf(q)
    return float(multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, ρ], [ρ, 1]]).cdf([z, z]) / q)

pairs = [("JPM", "BAC", "JPM·BAC\n(two banks)"),
         ("JPM", "KO", "JPM·KO\n(bank · staple)"),
         ("JPM", "DUK", "JPM·DUK\n(bank · utility)")]
labels, data, gauss = [], [], []
for x, y, lab in pairs:
    xv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[x].to_numpy()
    yv: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R[y].to_numpy()
    ρ = np.corrcoef(xv, yv)[0, 1]                 # the pair's exact correlation
    labels.append(lab)
    data.append(cocrash_fraction(xv, yv) * 100)
    gauss.append(gaussian_cocrash(ρ) * 100)

xs = np.arange(len(pairs)); w = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
ax.bar(xs - w / 2, gauss, w, color=COOL, label="a Gaussian with the same correlation")
ax.bar(xs + w / 2, data, w, color=CRASH, label="what actually happens")
ax.axhline(10, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)")
for i, (g, d) in enumerate(zip(gauss, data)):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(i + w / 2, d), xytext=(i + w / 2, g),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.1))
    ax.text(i + w / 2 + 0.04, (g + d) / 2, f"+{d - g:.0f}", fontsize=9, color=INK, va="center")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel("co-crash (%)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 80)
ax.set_title("Even a Gaussian fit to the exact correlation under-counts joint crashes",
             fontsize=11.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Reconciling the Headline "56%"
The same `cocrash_fraction` you see here is what the
[gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) and
[uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) labs report — there on a *controlled*
synthetic co-crashing pair, where it lands near **56%**.  On real bank pairs it is
even higher (~70%); on a bank-utility pair it falls to ~30% — lower, but in this
crisis-spanning sample even utilities are dragged well above independence.  One
definition, three datasets:

| Pair | Co-crash | |
|---|---|---|
| Synthetic co-crashing pair (the labs) | ~56% | the teaching example |
| Real bank pair (JPM, BAC) | ~70% | contagion in the wild |
| Real bank-utility pair (JPM, DUK) | ~30% | dragged down in crises |
| Independent baseline | ~10% | the threshold itself |

The number is only meaningful next to its definition and its data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why This Drives the Course
Pearson correlation already sees the bank block.  What it *misses* is that the
co-movement **concentrates in the tail** — the days you most need diversification
are the days it vanishes.  Catching that is the job of the
[dependence](../dependence/index.qmd) measures and the reason Gaussian risk models
fail in the [uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd) chapter.
:::

---

## What the Labs Reload From Here

The information-theoretic "Venn" labs — mutual information and total correlation
between multidimensional blocks — **reload** the blocks defined above rather than
re-deriving them. Below is the single, copy-pasteable recipe they start from:
load the returns, build the sector blocks from the metadata, and build the
real-toy `[JPM, BAC] · [XOM, CVX]` block.

```{python}
#| label: reload-recipe
from lectures import datasets

R = datasets.load_returns()                 # (n_days, 14) panel of daily returns
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta()          # ticker → label, sector

# Sector blocks: each sector is one multidimensional variable.
sector_cols = {
    sec: meta.loc[meta.sector == sec, "ticker"].tolist()
    for sec in meta.sector.unique()
}
X_banks:  Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"]  = R[sector_cols["Banks"]]    # (n_days, 5)
X_energy: Float[Array, "n_days d_energy"] = R[sector_cols["Energy"]]   # (n_days, 2)
X_tech:   Float[Array, "n_days d_tech"]   = R[sector_cols["Tech"]]     # (n_days, 3)

# The real-toy block: 2 banks vs 2 energy majors — small enough to read by hand.
x: Float[Array, "n_days d_x"] = R[["JPM", "BAC"]]    # (n_days, 2)
y: Float[Array, "n_days d_y"] = R[["XOM", "CVX"]]    # (n_days, 2)

print("sector blocks:",
      {k: R[v].shape for k, v in sector_cols.items()})
print("real-toy block:  x", x.shape, " y", y.shape)
pd.concat([x, y], axis=1).head(3).round(4)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Lab Contract
The information-Venn labs **reload these exact blocks** from the one-line recipe
above and *do not re-derive them*. The two halves of the contract:

- **Sector blocks** (`X_banks`, `X_energy`, `X_tech`, …) are the full
  multidimensional variables for within-block redundancy
  ($T(X_\text{banks})$) and between-block coupling
  ($I(X_\text{banks}; X_\text{energy})$).
- **The real-toy block** `x = R[["JPM","BAC"]]`, `y = R[["XOM","CVX"]]` is the
  small "toy examples of real data" rung — four columns you can read by hand,
  with the structure already visible in the 4×4 block above.

The **only** lab-specific extra step allowed is **subsampling** (~500 rows) for
the $O(n^2)$ estimators (kNN mutual information, RBIG), e.g.
`x.sample(500, random_state=0)`. Everything upstream of that — selection,
sectoring, the real-toy pairing — is owned here.

Three labs reload from this chapter:

- [Tool 2 · Information](../dependence/labs/lab-tool2-information.qmd) — mutual
  information between blocks.
- [Tool 3 · Windows](../dependence/labs/lab-tool3-windows.qmd) — block dependence
  through rolling windows.
- [Tool 3 · Mutual Information](../gaussianization/labs/lab-tool3-mutual-information.qmd)
  — MI via Gaussianization on these blocks.
:::
